newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch air trade bodies push for night ban review.
newsitem.headline: Dutch air trade bodies push for night ban review.

text.p: The Dutch airfreight shippers' organisation (EVO) and air transport association (ATAN)said they are joining forces to urge the government to review a ban on noisy night-time flights from Schiphol airport.

The ban, starting tonight, was backed yesterday by the Dutch government. It will stop aircraft such as the McDonnell Douglas DC-10 and Boeing in its 747-100, 200, 300 and SP versions, from taking off between 2300 and 0600 local time (2100 and 0400 gmt).

The government said that these measures are not enough and has given Schiphol until September 1 to come up with tougher measures. If not, the government will consider closing all or part of the airport, the transport ministry said.
The two organisations said the Dutch government should consider the likely consequences of the ban on the country's industry and employment.
Speaking to Reuters, EVO spokesman, Hans Leijgraaff, said "Where does this (ban) leave Schiphol in its bid to become a leading airport?"
He added that it was "incredible" that the transport minister should now call for even tougher measures and that large hi-tech exporters have already been in contact on the issue.
Companies are worried that this means there will be less choice as carriers will leave:"We could lose El Al and Polar Air and other carriers .....with one strike it is all over, ," Leijgraaff added.
There is also the very real danger that shippers will relocate, he said.
One shipper that specialises in hi-tech products to the Middle East and Africa established in Amsterdam in the last two years and is extremely worried, said Leijgraaff.

Previous industry estimates suggest Schiphol will lose at least 30,000 tonnes this year as a result of the ban rising to a loss of between 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes in 1998. The airport handled some 1.3 million tonnes in 1996 and 566,461 tonnes in January-June 1997.
And as about a third of the lost traffic will be Dutch-originating cargo, that means some 10,000 tonnes this year and 30,000 tonnes will have to go to other airports, Leijgraff said.
"These cargoes have to go by air, they cannot go by sea ....if this traffic all goes via other airports there will be more road traffic, thus more road pollution."

The EVO has written to all the Dutch political parties urging them not to push for futher measures and to take into account the country's industry. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
